scope: Only previously verified General Economics revisions and the 22 authorized post-verification question changes.

before.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

after.feedback: A consumption gain is the difference between the post-trade bundle and the pre-trade, or autarky, bundle. Specialization output and an exchange rate do not identify that missing baseline, so different autarky bundles could imply different numerical gains. Gains can be measured when the required consumption information is supplied.

before.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

after.feedback: With increasing opportunity cost, producing more of a good requires giving up progressively more of the other good. Reallocation can create gains while relative marginal costs differ, but the rising cost can make further specialization unattractive before either producer specializes completely. Absolute productivity alone does not determine that stopping point.

options: Malik, because he can make more videos.
Rina, because one poster costs her 0.5 video while it costs Malik 1 video.
Malik, because one poster costs him fewer posters.
Neither, because comparative advantage requires equal productivity.
before.feedback: Rina gives up fewer videos per poster, so she has the comparative advantage in posters.

options: Malik, because one poster costs him 0.5 video while it costs Rina 1 video.
Rina, because one poster costs her 0.5 video while it costs Malik 1 video.
Malik, because one poster costs him 1 video while it costs Rina 2 videos.
Neither, because one poster costs each of them 1 video at their stated output rates.
after.feedback: Rina gives up 4/8 = 0.5 video per poster, while Malik gives up 6/6 = 1 video per poster. Rina therefore has the lower opportunity cost of posters. Using 8/4 reverses the units to posters per video; swapping the producers or assuming equal costs also gives the wrong comparison.

options: Entry guarantees every firm the same cost.
Entry makes demand disappear.
Entry lets one firm set the market price.
Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.
before.feedback: Entry expands market supply and puts downward pressure on unusually high economic profits.

options: Economic profits attract new sellers, reducing market supply as existing firms divide sales among more rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, lowering each entrant’s costs until all firms share the same cost curve.
Economic profits attract new sellers, raising market demand as buyers redistribute purchases among rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.
after.feedback: Profit opportunities attract entrants when entry is easy. Their additional supply puts downward pressure on price and economic profits. Redistributing sales does not itself increase market demand, and entry does not make firms’ production costs identical.

options: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
Every restaurant must be a pure price taker.
Product differentiation eliminates all competition.
Many sellers guarantee identical products.
before.feedback: Competition can exist by degree; differentiation gives firms some price discretion.

options: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.
after.feedback: Many restaurants can compete for customers even when differentiated experiences give individual sellers some price discretion. Differentiation means the strict identical-product price-taking benchmark need not hold, but competing restaurants can still constrain each other’s prices.

options: Free entry guarantees price taking.
Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
Network effects have no effect on market power.
The largest platform must have the lowest opportunity cost.
before.feedback: Entrants may be allowed but unable to attract users when network effects reinforce the incumbent.

options: Legal freedom to enter makes the incumbent face perfectly elastic demand despite its user network.
Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
Network effects remove the incumbent’s advantage because every entrant can start with an equally valuable user network.
The incumbent’s user advantage implies formal entry is restricted, so the premise of free entry cannot hold.
after.feedback: Permission to enter does not ensure that a new platform can attract enough users to compete effectively. When a platform becomes more valuable as its user base grows, the incumbent’s network can be an entry obstacle even without legal restrictions. That advantage does not establish perfectly elastic demand or equal starting networks.

options: Demand rises if the income effect is larger than the substitute-price effect
Demand falls if the substitute-price effect is larger than the income effect
Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
before.feedback: Higher income raises demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute lowers it. Effect sizes are required.

options: Demand rises because higher income and a cheaper substitute both increase demand for movie tickets.
Demand falls because the cheaper substitute lowers ticket demand while income does not shift demand for a normal good.
Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
after.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute reduces demand for movie tickets. The effects oppose each other and their relative sizes are not supplied, so the net shift cannot be determined. These are demand shifters, not changes caused by the ticket’s own price.

before.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

after.feedback: A subsidy changes the payoff from an action. People may adjust related choices as well as the behavior the policy targets, creating effects the designer did not intend. Those responses belong in the policy’s benefit-and-cost analysis even when the subsidy is enforced as designed.

options: Only the total cost, because distribution does not matter
Making the policy tradeoffs explicit
Whether the policy is efficient enough to eliminate all value judgments
A single overall result without identifying who bears the costs.
before.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

options: The combined cost alone, without showing how it is divided between the two groups.
The costs each group bears and the tradeoffs between the policy alternatives.
The adviser’s preferred outcome alone, without showing the costs of other choices.
The taxpayers’ costs alone, without including the costs borne by commuters.
after.feedback: An informative comparison identifies which costs fall on commuters and which fall on taxpayers, and how those costs change across policy alternatives. A single total can conceal the distribution of costs and the tradeoffs facing the decision maker.

before.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

after.feedback: Enforcement and administration use scarce staff time, equipment and other resources. A feasible policy estimate must include those implementation costs when comparing benefits with costs. Omitting them can overstate net benefits even if the policy’s stated goal is desirable.

before.q: Which example is an unintended response to an incentive?

after.q: Which statement describes an unintended response to an incentive?

before.feedback: Good incentive analysis asks whose behavior changes, at what margin, and with what side effects.

after.feedback: The same fee can change the relative attractiveness of an action by different amounts for different people. Someone with a close substitute may switch, while someone with few alternatives or a high benefit from the action may continue. An unchanged choice does not mean the fee created no incentive.

before.feedback: Good incentive analysis asks whose behavior changes, at what margin, and with what side effects.

after.feedback: People who would take the action without the subsidy can receive a payment without changing their behavior. Those payments are inframarginal: they support actions already planned rather than inducing additional ones. The policy’s additional impact depends on how many people change their choice because of the subsidy.

options: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
It creates a gap between two domestic currencies
It makes imports free
It sets producer surplus to zero
before.feedback: In the small-country model, the tariff creates a wedge between the world price and the higher domestic price paid and received in the protected market.

options: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
It creates a gap between domestic quantity supplied and domestic quantity demanded, measured as tax per unit.
It creates a gap between the government’s total tariff receipts and the per-unit price paid for imports.
It creates a gap between the lower domestic buyer price and the unchanged world price after the tariff.
after.feedback: In the small-country importing model, a tariff raises the domestic price above the world price while imports continue. That price difference is the per-unit tax wedge. The import quantity and total tariff revenue are different measures, and the tariff does not lower the domestic buyer price.

options: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
All trade restrictions have identical distributional effects
Only quotas create deadweight loss
Tariffs never affect domestic producers
before.feedback: Policy evaluation must track both efficiency distortions and the destination of rents or revenue.

options: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
Two policies with matching price and quantity effects must give their revenue or rents to the same recipients.
Two policies with matching import quantities must raise equal government revenue, even when quota licenses are given away.
Two policies can raise the same domestic price, but only the quota distorts domestic production and consumption.
after.feedback: An equivalent tariff and binding quota can produce similar prices and quantities, yet tariff revenue goes to government while quota rents go to the holders of import rights unless those rights are auctioned. Both can distort production and consumption. Policy design must therefore track who receives revenue or rents as well as efficiency effects.

options: Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers
Retaliation lowers every domestic price
Retaliation automatically refunds tariff revenue
Retaliation guarantees more trade
before.feedback: Retaliation can spread losses to export industries.

options: Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers
Trading partners may tax imports from the country, but the proceeds go into the original country’s treasury.
Trading partners may tax imports from the country, making its goods cheaper for foreign customers to buy.
Trading partners may restrict imports from the country, increasing sales opportunities for the country’s exporters.
after.feedback: Retaliation can restrict sales of the country’s exports in foreign markets. Export producers and their workers can therefore lose business in addition to the costs created by the original tariff.

before.q: A nonrefundable fee has already been paid. It should affect the current decision:
before.feedback: A cost is sunk only when it cannot be recovered or changed.

after.q: A fee has already been paid, but its refund terms have not yet been checked. When should it affect the current decision?
after.feedback: Check whether the current choice changes how much of the fee can be recovered. A refund available under one choice but not another is relevant; a payment that cannot be recovered or changed is sunk. Having paid the fee does not by itself establish that it is irrelevant, and a desire to recover past spending is not a marginal benefit.

before.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

after.feedback: A prediction about soda sales is a testable claim about a particular product market. A recommendation about national health includes a judgment about desired outcomes and policy tradeoffs. Micro-versus-macro scope and positive-versus-normative reasoning are separate distinctions; a national policy recommendation does not make every underlying claim macroeconomic or normative.

options: PPF1 determines society's preferred output combination without preference information
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B is now inside the new frontier; higher welfare is not established by the shift alone
B remains efficient because it was efficient on PPF0
The unchanged output proves the outward shift cannot represent added capacity
Capacity expanded, and PPF1 identifies the preferred output combination; unchanged production at B therefore establishes that welfare has increased.
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B is now inside the new frontier; higher welfare is not established by the shift alone
Capacity expanded, but unchanged B remains on the efficient frontier; its earlier efficiency establishes that resources are still fully employed.
Capacity stayed unchanged because production remains at B; the shift to PPF1 changes the selected output mix rather than the feasible set.
Current supply increases if the technology effect exceeds the inventory-withholding effect.
The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
Current supply decreases if the inventory-withholding effect exceeds the technology effect.
Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.
before.feedback: Better technology shifts supply right, while withholding output for future sale shifts current supply left.

options: Current supply increases because improved technology and storing output for future sale both add to current market supply.
The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
Current supply decreases because the expected future price rises sharply, which establishes that withholding outweighs the technology improvement.
Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.
after.feedback: Better technology increases current supply, while withholding output for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. The word “sharply” does not quantify the withholding effect relative to the technology effect, so the net direction remains uncertain. Neither determinant is a change in the product’s current price along a fixed curve.

options: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
Buyers and sellers split the burden equally because the tax amount is fixed
Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
